articles.summary: Democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier is projected to win Rep. Adriano Espaillat’s (D) seat representing New York in the House, according to Decision Desk HQ, in a win for the Big Apple’s socialist movement. Avila Chevalier defeated Espaillat in a contentious summer primary after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a fellow democratic socialist, endorsed…
articles.body:
Democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier is projected to win Rep. Adriano Espaillat’s (D) seat representing New York in the House, according to Decision Desk HQ, in a win for the Big Apple’s socialist movement.

Avila Chevalier defeated Espaillat in a contentious summer primary after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a fellow democratic socialist, endorsed her over the five-term incumbent.

DDHQ projected Avila Chevalier’s win at 9 p.m. EST Tuesday.

The political newcomer sailed to a general election victory in the solidly blue 13th Congressional District, which makes up parts of Harlem, Washington Heights and the Bronx.

The primary was a squabble between progressives. Espaillat, the first member of Congress to have previously been an immigrant without legal status, was backed by left-wing Reps. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and others in the Congressional Progressive Caucus.

But Avila Chevalier, who organized protests against Israel at Columbia University, attacked Espaillat for accepting support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee as she called for an end to U.S. support for Israel.

In September, Avila Chevalier was among several protesters who were arrested during a demonstration against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech at the United Nations headquarters in Manhattan.

Avila Chevalier is one of two members of the Democratic Socialists of America who are expected to represent the Empire State in the House, alongside New York State Assembly member Claire Valdez, who’s on track to replace outgoing Rep. Nydia Velázquez (D) in the 7th Congressional District.

images.caption: Darializa Avila Chevalier, U.S. Democratic House candidate for New York, center, speaks during a rally with Columbia postdoctoral workers at Haven Plaza at Columbia University Medical Center in New York on June 30, 2026.

articles.body:
New York State Assembly member Micah Lasher (D) will win the open Manhattan-based seat to succeed longtime Rep. Jerry Nadler (D-N.Y.), Decision Desk HQ has projected.

Lasher defeated Republican Caroline Shinkle, an attorney, in New York’s 12th District, a win that came as no surprise in a solidly blue area. He worked in New York politics for years before he was elected to the state Assembly in 2024.

The seat became open after Nadler, who has served in the House for more than 30 years, announced he would not run for reelection.

Lasher prevailed in a crowded Democratic primary against fellow state Assembly member Alex Bores and two high-profile figures — Jack Schlossberg and George Conway.

Among Lasher’s supporters in the primary included Nadler himself. Lasher previously served as an aide to the congressman.

images.caption: Micah Lasher, the Democratic candidate in New York’s 12th Congressional District, speaks during “NY-12 for Congress: Candidate Forum” at 92NY, on April 15, 2026, in New York.

articles.body:
Colorado Sen. John Hickenlooper (D) is projected to win a second term in the upper chamber, according to Decision Desk HQ.

He defeated Republican Mark Baisley, a state lawmaker, for the solid-blue seat. Hickenlooper was first elected to Capitol Hill in 2020, and he serves on the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committees, among others.

The Senate Democrat previously served as the mayor of Denver from 2003 to 2011 and governor of the Centennial State from 2011 to 2019. He unsuccessfully ran for president in 2020, ending his campaign to instead run for Senate.

Hickenlooper was the favorite to win in the blue state. A Colorado Republican hasn’t been elected to the Senate since 2014.

articles.title: Austin Rogers wins House race to succeed retiring Dunn in Florida
articles.summary: Austin Rogers (R) is projected to defeat Amanda Marie Green (D) in Florida’s 2nd District, according to Decision Desk HQ. Rogers will succeed retiring Rep. Neal Dunn (R-Fla.). Dunn, 73, will depart the lower chamber at the end of his fifth term representing the Panhandle-based district. Rogers led Green by about 4 percentage points with…
articles.body:
Austin Rogers (R) is projected to defeat Amanda Marie Green (D) in Florida’s 2nd District, according to Decision Desk HQ .

Rogers will succeed retiring Rep. Neal Dunn (R-Fla.). Dunn, 73, will depart the lower chamber at the end of his fifth term representing the Panhandle-based district.

Rogers led Green by about 4 percentage points with 95 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 9:02 p.m. Tuesday.

By virtue of his victory over Green, a former U.S. Agency for International Development contractor, Rogers clinches a return to Capitol Hill.

The Republican lawyer was a legal counsel for the Senate Judiciary Committee from the fall of 2023 to mid-2025. He was then Florida Sen. Rick Scott’s (R) general counsel for less than a year, before launching his congressional campaign in January.

Rogers emerged from a crowded Republican field in the August primary , capturing the nomination over the likes of businessman Keith Gross and Florida GOP Chair Evan Power.

He then defeated Green, a result election handicappers anticipated going into Election Day.

Dunn also won the district by more than 20 percentage points in all but one of his five victories from 2016 through 2024.

Rogers aligned himself with Dunn on the campaign trail, saying in August the outgoing lawmaker “has set a high standard for conservative leadership” while in Congress.

He also vowed to be a “reliable” vote for President Trump’s agenda and called Trump the “most consequential President of our lifetime” on his campaign website.

images.caption: Rep. Neal Dunn (R-Fla.) is seen during the annual Friends of Ireland Luncheon at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on March 17, 2026.

articles.title: Democrat Paige Cognetti defeats Bresnahan, flipping key House seat

Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton, clinched the district running on an anti-corruption message, marking a key pickup for Democrats — who need to flip three GOP-held seats to win control of…
articles.body:
Democrat Paige Cognetti is projected to defeat first-term incumbent Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R) in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton, clinched the district running on an anti-corruption message, marking a key pickup for Democrats — who need to flip three GOP-held seats to win control of the House.

With 30 percent of the ballots counted around 9:10 p.m. EST, Cognetti had secured 70 percent of the vote, DDHQ reported .

Democrats hammered Bresnahan over stock trades he’s made since taking office, although his office says an outside financial institution managed his investments.

Republicans flipped the district in 2024, as Bresnahan knocked off longtime Democratic Rep. Matt Cartwright.

Cook Political Report rated the district a tossup after initially saying it leaned Republican.

It was one of the most competitive this cycle and attracted some of the highest amounts of outside spending, as both parties poured cash into the race.

images.caption: Scranton, Pa., Mayor Paige Cognetti speaks during a campaign event for former President Biden in Scranton on April 16, 2024.

articles.body:
Wyoming Rep. Harriet Hageman (R) is projected to ascend to the upper chamber, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Hageman defeated Democrat James W. Byrd in the race to succeed Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R), who opted not to seek a second term .

The House Republican served two terms in the lower chamber after defeating former GOP Rep. Liz Cheney in the 2022 GOP primary. A staunch ally of President Trump, Hageman notched his endorsement in 2025.

“I know Harriet well, and she is a TOTAL WINNER!” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “Harriet has ALWAYS delivered for Wyoming, and will continue to do so in the United States Senate.”

A lawyer by trade, Hageman serves on the lower chamber’s Natural Resources and Judiciary Committees. She unsuccessfully ran for governor in 2018.

Harriet Hageman (R-Wyo.) speaks during a press conference outside the Department of Agriculture in Washington, D.C., on April 30, 2025, to discuss a recent court decision in-favor of Charles and Heather Maude of Caputa, S.D., in a 2024 land dispute. The Maude’s had fencing on 25 acres of property that blocked access of the Buffalo Gap National Grasslands.

articles.title: Democrats seize House control from Republicans
articles.summary: Democrats on Tuesday seized control of the U.S. House, flipping the chamber after four years in the minority wilderness to usher in a new era of divided government, Decision Desk HQ projects. The change will have immediate repercussions for the workings of Washington next year, slamming the brakes on President Trump’s legislative agenda and setting…
articles.body:
Democrats on Tuesday seized control of the U.S. House, flipping the chamber after four years in the minority wilderness to usher in a new era of divided government, Decision Desk HQ projects.

The change will have immediate repercussions for the workings of Washington next year, slamming the brakes on President Trump’s legislative agenda and setting the stage for countless clashes between the House and White House over everything from immigration enforcement and government spending to Trump’s global tariffs and the Iran war.

Democrats have vowed to launch an exhaustive list of investigations into Trump and his inner circle, featuring deep dives into the Jeffrey Epstein scandal; the violence that’s accompanied Trump’s deportation surge; and the president’s personal and family finances, which have ballooned since his return to office last year.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is expected to be the next Speaker, has said those investigations will begin immediately.

“Our promise to the country in the new Congress is that, beginning on Day 1, we’re going to hold the crooks accountable,” Jeffries said heading into the elections.

Democrats have already started many of those probes in the current Congress. But they will escalate next year given the broad new authorities Democrats will have in the majority, including the powers to control the floor agenda, dictate committee hearings and issue subpoenas in seeking documents and witness testimony. Trump’s Cabinet leaders and family members, Democrats say, will be high on the list.

Democrats are also readying an aggressive legislative agenda featuring efforts to bring down the high cost of consumer goods — for everything from groceries and gas to housing and healthcare. In the earliest weeks, that’s likely to include legislation to restore the ObamaCare subsidies that expired in January and reverse the Medicaid cuts enacted by Republicans last year.

Those bills are not expected to become law, since Trump will still be in the White House with his veto pen. But they could prove to be tough votes for vulnerable Republican lawmakers, and they will provide Democrats with a concrete policy track record heading into the 2028 elections.

The midterm cycle is historically tough on the party that controls the White House, and the trend was only exacerbated this year by the volatility of the economy, an unpopular war in Iran and the high cost of living, which has dogged Trump’s return to the White House. Heading into Election Day, the president’s approval ratings were at historic lows, creating challenges for GOP candidates even in some districts Trump won easily just two years ago.

Sensing a difficult environment, Trump and his allies had sought to cushion the Republicans’ House majority by pressing GOP-led states to redraw their maps in favor of Republican candidates.

That effort allowed Republicans to pick up a few seats that otherwise would have gone to the Democrats, but it wasn’t enough to insulate them from the wave of restive voters who appeared to treat the midterms as a referendum on Trump — and an opportunity to put a check on the president’s executive power.

The Democrats’ victory puts Jeffries in line to make history as the country’s first Black Speaker, a vote that will take place on the House floor on Jan. 3.

Immediately below Jeffries, the party’s leadership roster is not likely to change: Rep. Katherine Clark (Mass.), the Democratic whip, is expected to remain the No. 2 Democrat as majority leader, while Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), the caucus chair, is expected to remain in the No. 3 spot as the new whip.

Beyond that, the Democrats’ ascension to the majority is likely to trigger a number of contested races for the lower rungs of the leadership ladder, including the caucus chair and vice chair positions, which will play an outsized role in communicating the Democrats’ message heading into the 2028 elections.

Democrats will confront their own unique challenges in the majority. Jeffries, in particular, will face a delicate balancing act in navigating between the competing demands of progressive and socialist Democrats clamoring for a more aggressive response to the Trump administration and more moderate members from competitive districts who are wary of the party moving too far to the left.

Across the aisle, the transition to the House minority forces Republicans to reassess their leadership and strategy heading into the next Congress.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has indicated that he wants to remain the party’s leader even in the minority, while House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) are both expected to launch bids for the minority leader role.

The coming weeks will be critical for Republicans as they race to advance as much of Trump’s agenda as possible before Democrats assume power. Key items on their list include the National Defense Authorization Act and legislation that would reauthorize funding for food and agricultural programs. That’s on top of legislation to fund the government and prevent a federal shutdown in mid-December.

Some Republicans also want to move a third reconciliation bill, a massive package of partisan priorities that would move on a special procedural track requiring no Democratic support. It’s unclear, however, if there will be an appetite to remain in Washington to do that work after the Republicans’ demoralizing losses on Tuesday.

articles.title: Democrat Zach Dembo projected to flip Kentucky House seat
articles.summary: Democrat Zach Dembo, a Navy veteran and former federal prosecutor, is projected to win Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), flipping a Republican-held seat in a major pickup for Democrats. Dembo was leading Republican Ralph Alvarado 55 percent to 41 percent with 92 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as…
articles.body:
Democrat Zach Dembo, a Navy veteran and former federal prosecutor, is projected to win Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), flipping a Republican-held seat in a major pickup for Democrats.

Dembo was leading Republican Ralph Alvarado 55 percent to 41 percent with 92 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 9:07 p.m. EST.

Dembo defeated Alvarado, a former Kentucky state senator and physician endorsed by President Trump, in the race to succeed Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.), who opted to run for the Senate.

The victory marks the first time a Democrat has won the central Kentucky seat since former Rep. Ben Chandler (D-Ky.), who lost his reelection bid to Barr in 2012.

The district, which includes Lexington and parts of central Kentucky, was initially expected to remain safely in Republican hands. Trump carried it by roughly 15 percentage points in 2024, while Barr won reelection that year by more than 26 points.

But the race grew increasingly competitive in the months leading up to Election Day. The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report moved the contest from “lean Republican” to “toss-up” in October as Democrats continued to mount a serious challenge for the open seat.

Dembo, who has never held elected office, previously served as a Navy Judge Advocate General’s Corps officer and as a federal prosecutor. He also spent some time working for Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D). He chose to resign from his role at the Justice Department under the Trump administration after viewing what he described as a shocking amount of corruption in Washington, D.C.

The Democrat defeated former Kentucky state Rep. Cherlynn Stevenson and several other Democrats in a crowded May primary.

Dembo described himself as a “Beshear Democrat,” seeking to build on the crossover appeal of the Democratic governor, who won his reelection bid in 2023 despite the state’s strong Republican lean.

Beshear, who stayed neutral during the primary, endorsed Dembo in the general election and campaigned alongside him in events leading up to the midterm elections. The campaign sought to tie Alvarado to former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin (R), who was defeated by Beshear in his reelection bid. Alvarado was Bevin’s running mate on that ticket.

Dembo’s campaign focused on affordability and accountability, criticizing Trump’s economic policies, including tariffs, while promising to fight corruption. He also sought to appeal to voters across party lines by highlighting his military service and law enforcement background.

images.caption: Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.) arrives to the Capitol in Washington, D.C., for the first votes of the week on Monday, April 28, 2025, following a two-week recess.

articles.title: Bottoms defeats Rick Jackson, turning Georgia governor’s office blue
articles.summary: Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) is projected to win the Georgia governor’s race over Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson — turning the Peach State’s highest office blue for the first time in more than two decades, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Bottoms led Jackson by about 11 points with 71 percent of…
articles.body:
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) is projected to win the Georgia governor’s race over Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson — turning the Peach State’s highest office blue for the first time in more than two decades, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) .

Bottoms led Jackson by about 11 points with 71 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ.

Bottoms, who served as a senior adviser to former President Biden, will become Georgia’s first Democratic governor since Roy Barnes left office in 2003 after one term. Before its recent run of GOP state leadership — which included term-limited outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp — Democrats filled the gubernatorial seat for more than a century.

Election handicappers Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball had each rated the race as a “toss-up” as recently as late October. Bottoms was also narrowly leading Jackson in a recent poll by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and University of Georgia.

The former Atlanta mayor got a boost when former President Obama joined her and Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) for a rally in late October.

It’s a tough loss for Republicans and President Trump, who endorsed Jackson in July and called him a “true champion for the people” at a rally in Cobb County. But the endorsement came after the president previously backed Lt. Gov. Burt Jones (R), who lost to Jackson in a primary runoff.

images.caption: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks during a rally ahead of the Georgia Primary Election on Oct. 17, 2026, in Atlanta.

articles.title: Jackley wins election for South Dakota’s sole House seat
articles.summary: South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley (R) is projected to win the state’s lone House seat, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), with Jackley defeating Democrat Nikki Gronli in the race to succeed Rep. Dusty Johnson (R-S.D.). Jackley, who has served two stints as the state’s top law enforcement official, will replace Johnson, who opted…
articles.body:
South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley (R) is projected to win the state’s lone House seat, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), with Jackley defeating Democrat Nikki Gronli in the race to succeed Rep. Dusty Johnson (R-S.D.).

Jackley, who has served two stints as the state’s top law enforcement official, will replace Johnson, who opted against seeking a fifth term in Congress to run for governor.

DDHQ called the race for Jackley when he led by 34 percentage points with 1 percent of the vote reported as of 9 p.m. EST.

The victory keeps the statewide congressional seat in Republican hands, where it has safely remained since 2011. South Dakota has not elected a Democrat to the House since former Rep. Stephanie Herseth Sandlin, who lost her reelection bid to former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in 2010.

The state has been a Republican stronghold in the Trump era. The president carried South Dakota by nearly 30 percentage points in 2024, while Johnson won reelection that year by a much wider 44-point margin against Democrat Sheryl Johnson.

Jackley held a significant advantage heading into the general election, with the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rating the race as “solid Republican.”

Jackley secured the Republican nomination in June, easily defeating James Bialota with more than 79 percent of the vote. His path to nomination became even easier after state Sen. Casey Crabtree dropped out of the race in February and threw his support behind Jackley.

He has spent much of his career in law enforcement, serving as U.S. attorney for South Dakota from 2006 to 2009 before being appointed state attorney general, a position he held until 2019.

Jackley returned to office in 2023 after winning the Republican nomination at the party’s state convention in 2022. He made an unsuccessful bid for governor in 2018, losing the Republican primary to Noem.

His Democratic opponent, Gronli, previously served as South Dakota’s state director of rural development for the Department of Agriculture. She secured her party’s nomination without a primary challenge after other Democratic candidates withdrew.

Jackley emphasized his experience as attorney general throughout his campaign, touting his record of pursuing criminal prosecution and presenting himself as a conservative focused on public safety and law enforcement while fighting drug trafficking and supporting border security.

images.caption: South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley leaves the U.S. Supreme Court, April 17, 2018, in Washington.

articles.title: Cowan clinches Georgia House seat held by retiring Loudermilk
articles.summary: Republican John Cowan, a neurosurgeon and small-business owner, is projected to win Georgia’s 11th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ, defeating Democratic Woodstock attorney Chris Harden in the open race. Cowan led Harden 53.8 percent to 46.2 percent with 76 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 9:17 p.m. EST Tuesday.…
articles.body:
Republican John Cowan, a neurosurgeon and small-business owner, is projected to win Georgia’s 11th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ, defeating Democratic Woodstock attorney Chris Harden in the open race.

Cowan led Harden 53.8 percent to 46.2 percent with 76 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 9:17 p.m. EST Tuesday.

Cowan will succeed retiring Rep. Barry Loudermilk (R-Ga.), who has represented the northwest Georgia district since 2015.

The district, which includes parts of Cobb, Cherokee, Bartow, Gordon and Pickens counties, has long been considered a Republican stronghold. President Trump carried it by roughly 23 percentage points in 2024, while Loudermilk won reelection that year by nearly 35 percentage points.

Trump threw his support behind the board-certified neurosurgeon in July, describing him as an “America First Patriot” who will “Advance Election Integrity” while promising to cut taxes and expand domestic energy production.

This is Cowan’s second run for Congress , after first seeking a House seat in 2020 in Georgia’s neighboring 14th Congressional District. He advanced to a Republican primary runoff before losing to former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.).

He returned to the campaign trail after Loudermilk announced that he would not seek reelection, entering a crowded seven-way Republican primary that included Loudermilk’s former chief of staff and preferred successor, Rob Adkerson.

Cowan emerged as the leading candidate in the May primary with nearly 43 percent of the vote, followed by Adkerson with about 22 percent. Former Georgia Public Service Commissioner Tricia Pridemore finished third, failing to advance to the runoff. Cowan ultimately went on to defeat Adkerson in the June runoff by a decisive 65 percent of the vote versus Adkerson’s 35 percent, securing the Republican nomination despite his opponent’s backing from Loudermilk.

The Georgia Republican has practiced medicine in Georgia for more than a decade. He graduated from Davidson College and earned his medical degree from Johns Hopkins University before completing his neurosurgery residency at the University of Michigan.

images.caption: John Cowan, the Republican candidate in the race for Georgia’s 11th Congressional District, speaks before President Trump arrives at a campaign rally on Oct. 24, 2026, in Perry, Ga.

articles.title: Buttigieg calls Trump’s Reflecting Pool press conference ‘symbol of incompetence’
articles.summary: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg called President Trump’s press conference Monday in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool a “symbol of incompetence.” “The fact that even after manipulating the districts, these districts are still competitive and may well vote Democratic in this election shows you just how far the priorities of the White House…
articles.body:
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg called President Trump’s press conference Monday in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool a “symbol of incompetence.”

“The fact that even after manipulating the districts, these districts are still competitive and may well vote Democratic in this election shows you just how far the priorities of the White House and the congressional Republicans have drifted away from the things Americans care about,” Buttigieg told Meidas Touch on Tuesday. “And I think it’s also telling that their closing arguments did nothing to help with that, right? At a moment where people were more concerned than ever about healthcare, gas prices, grocery prices.”

“Yet the president making his closing argument, standing in front of the Reflecting Pool which is kind of a giant symbol of the incompetence and the corruption and dishonesty of the administration,” he continued.

Buttigieg said that Trump’s decision to deliver his midterms closing argument at the Reflecting Pool was a “powerful message” to voters across the country — including in conservative areas — that the president “just doesn’t care about them.”

“And voters care about that and want to send a message back,” the former Transportation Secretary concluded.

Trump’s speech at the Reflecting Pool on Monday focused largely on the landmark’s reopening, notably not mentioning Tuesday’s elections until roughly 20 minutes into his speech.

“As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime,” he said. “The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history.”

Trump also reiterated his promise of doling out $5,000 checks to all American adults if the GOP maintains control of Congress, adding that his last few midterm rallies were “full of love.”

This comes as Buttigieg and other national Democrats were put on the defensive following the GOP’s efforts to redistrict some key congressional districts. He became heavily involved with campaigning for a number of candidates across the country in an effort to boost the party’s odds to regain control of the upper and lower chamber.

Buttigieg — a former presidential candidate — is also among the top contenders for the 2028 Democratic presidential primaries.

images.caption: Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg speaks at a General Election Kickoff Rally for Michigan Democrats at Renaissance High School on Aug. 7, 2026, in Detroit.

articles.title: Gaines set to succeed Georgia’s Collins in House
articles.summary: Republican Houston Gaines is projected to win Georgia’s 10th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ, defeating Democrat Pamela DeLancy in the race for the open House seat. Gaines, a Georgia state representative endorsed by President Trump, will succeed Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who gave up his House seat to run for Senate. Gaines’s victory…
articles.body:
Republican Houston Gaines is projected to win Georgia’s 10th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ, defeating Democrat Pamela DeLancy in the race for the open House seat.

Gaines, a Georgia state representative endorsed by President Trump, will succeed Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who gave up his House seat to run for Senate .

Gaines’s victory came with little surprise. The district, which includes Athens and stretches across parts of northeast and central Georgia, is considered a Republican stronghold and hasn’t elected a Democrat since former Rep. Don Johnson Jr. (D-Ga.) in 1992. Collins easily won reelection in 2024 with more than 63 percent of the vote.

Gaines, an Athens native, has served in the Georgia House since 2019 and is vice chair of the state House Republican Caucus. He represents portions of Barrow, Clarke, Jackson and Oconee counties.

The Republican won a three-way primary in May against film executive Ryan Millsap and Jeffrey Baker, with Trump’s endorsement helping him secure the party’s nomination.

Gaines campaigned on cracking down on illegal immigration, supporting law enforcement, cutting government spending and lowering taxes. He also emphasized his record in the state legislature, including legislation aimed at restricting cashless bail and supporting state immigration enforcement policies.

The Republican has pointed to the 2024 murder of nursing student Laken Riley in Athens as a reason for tougher immigration laws. Riley was attacked and killed while jogging by a Venezuelan migrant, and her death became a flash point in the national immigration debate.

Outside politics, Gaines works in business development at Carter Engineering, an engineering firm in northeast Georgia. He graduated from the University of Georgia, where he studied political science and economics.

His opponent DeLancy, a retired Army colonel and registered nurse, won the Democratic nomination over Lexy Doherty, who unsuccessfully challenged Collins in 2024.

images.caption: Georgia state Rep. Houston Gaines (R), the Republican nominee in the race for Georgia’s 10th Congressional District, speaks before President Trump arrives at a campaign rally on Oct. 24, 2026, in Perry, Ga.

articles.title: Landsman fends off GOP challenge in purple Ohio House district
articles.summary: Rep. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) is projected to fend off his President Trump-backed GOP challenger Eric Conroy to keep his seat in Ohio’s 1st Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Landsman faced a tough challenger in Conroy, a former CIA officer and Air Force veteran whom Vice President Vance told reporters he voted for…
articles.body:
Rep. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) is projected to fend off his President Trump-backed GOP challenger Eric Conroy to keep his seat in Ohio’s 1st Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Landsman faced a tough challenger in Conroy, a former CIA officer and Air Force veteran whom Vice President Vance told reporters he voted for in the primaries.

DDHQ projected that Landsman defeated Conroy by 11.97 points with 51 percent of the race called at 9:28 p.m. EST.

Landsman has represented the district since 2023, but a mid-decade redistricting push put his seat in contention. Landsman’s district shifted toward Republicans as Trump lost the district by 6 points in 2024, but under the new map, he would have won it by 2.5 points, according to the Cook Political Report .

He was criticized by his Democratic colleagues earlier this year for crossing the aisle to vote against Reps. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) Iran war powers resolution .

Landsman said at the time that his vote was not in support of Trump acting in the conflict against Iran without congressional oversight.

“Congress declares war, and Congress must fund it. These are targeted strikes on core military assets — missiles, rockets, drones, ships,” he said, according to the Ohio Capital Journal . “I support targeted strikes to destroy Iran’s missiles and bombs to stop the regime from taking more lives.”

Landsman backed an alternative Iran war powers resolution with other lawmakers that would have given the Trump administration a 30-day timeline to pull forces out of the region or face another congressional vote.

He campaigned on capping the cost of prescription drug prices, investing in childcare providers, codifying Roe v. Wade and improving public infrastructure, according to his campaign website .

While on the campaign trail, he denied allegations levied in attack ads that accused him of insider trading and violating disclosure laws.

“I’m one of only a few members of Congress that sold their stocks,” Landsman said, according to an interview with ABC affiliate WCPO .

Landsman also remains one of the only members of Congress to sell all of his individual stocks. He backed the Restore Trust in Government Act , which would ban members of Congress from owning, buying or selling stocks.

articles.title: South Carolina’s Climer wins election to succeed Norman in House
articles.summary: Republican Wes Climer is projected to succeed South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman (R) in the House, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Climer was leading with 51 percent of the vote, with 78 percent of the total reported, by DDHQ as of 9:29 p.m. EST Tuesday. Climer, a state senator, defeated Democrat Mallory Dittmer to…
articles.body:
Republican Wes Climer is projected to succeed South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman (R) in the House, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Climer was leading with 51 percent of the vote, with 78 percent of the total reported, by DDHQ as of 9:29 p.m. EST Tuesday.

Climer, a state senator, defeated Democrat Mallory Dittmer to clinch the ruby-red district. Norman unsuccessfully ran for both governor and Senate this summer.

The incumbent backed Climer for the 5th District seat in the northern portion of the Palmetto State.

The lawmaker-elect tendered his resignation from the state Senate — effective Election Day — this summer, as election forecasters rated the contest as “safe” for the GOP.

Norman was first elected in 2017 after President Trump nominated then-Rep. Mick Mulvaney (R-S.C.) to lead the Office of Management and Budget. He is a member of the hard-line House Freedom Caucus.

Norman made headlines in the lead-up to the midterms amid his criticism of Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.). Norman lost to Darline Graham by about 5 percentage points in a special GOP primary for Senate after her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), died unexpectedly over the summer.

The House Republican indicated he would vote for Darline Graham over Democrat Annie Andrews, but he said his family was unlikely to do the same.

articles.title: Trump-backed Mike Mazzei wins Oklahoma governor’s race
articles.summary: Former Oklahoma state Sen. Mike Mazzei (R) is projected to defeat Democratic state Rep. Cyndi Munson in the Sooner State’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Mazzei, who previously served as the state’s secretary of budget under Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt, will succeed the term-limited governor, keeping the office in GOP hands. With…
articles.body:
Former Oklahoma state Sen. Mike Mazzei (R) is projected to defeat Democratic state Rep. Cyndi Munson in the Sooner State’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) .

Mazzei, who previously served as the state’s secretary of budget under Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt, will succeed the term-limited governor, keeping the office in GOP hands.

With just more than half of the ballots counted, Mazzei had almost 55 percent of the vote, DDHQ reported.

The Republican secured his party’s nomination in August after narrowly defeating Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond in a primary runoff.

President Trump endorsed Mazzei ahead of the runoff , while Drummond campaigned on his record as attorney general and sought to appeal to Trump’s supporters. The president also traveled to Oklahoma in October to rally Republicans behind the GOP hopeful.

Mazzei, a financial planner, made tax cuts a central part of his campaign. He proposed eliminating property taxes for seniors and veterans, reducing income taxes and cutting federal spending.

He also campaigned on improving education, restricting foreign ownership of land in the state and reducing government regulations.

Munson, the Democratic leader in the Oklahoma House, focused her campaign on affordability, public education and access to healthcare. She also opposed additional income tax cuts that she argued would disproportionately benefit wealthy residents.

The candidates differed over property tax relief, with Munson raising concerns that broad reductions could undermine funding for public schools and county services.

DDHQ rated the seat as “safe” for Republicans ahead of Election Day.

articles.body:
New Mexico Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D) is projected to win a second term in the upper chamber, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Luján defeated Republican Larry Marker in the blue state. The incumbent previously served in the House, representing the state’s 3rd District from 2009-21. He also chaired the House Democrats’ campaign arm for four years.

He serves on a number of committees, including the Agriculture, Nutrition and Forestry panel as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee.

Prior to federal service, Luján was the chair of the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission and worked in the state’s cultural affairs department.

His father, Ben Luján Sr., served as Speaker of the state House, working in the lower chamber for decades.

articles.body:
Democrat Bob Brooks is projected to defeat incumbent GOP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie to flip Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ.

With 19 percent of precincts reporting, Brooks is leading 65 percent to 34.9 percent.

Brooks ousted Mackenzie after only one term in the House and will flip the district from Republican to Democrat.

The Democrat had spent 20 years as a firefighter in Bethlehem and also runs Brooks Lawn Care, a family-operated snow removal business that he started in 2013. He retired from his firefighter role last year.

Brooks received endorsements from top Democrats in the Keystone State including Gov. Josh Shapiro, Lt. Gov. Austin Davis and Reps. Chris Deluzio, Madeleine Dean and Chrissy Houlahan.

Over his two decades as a firefighter, he worked to negotiate better contracts, affordable healthcare and safer working conditions.

Brooks has focused his campaign on raising minimum wage, building out healthcare, securing the border and protecting the community from data centers.

articles.title: Bennett ousts Kean Jr. in battleground New Jersey House race
articles.summary: Former healthcare executive Rebecca Bennett will defeat Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R) in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District, capitalizing on what many Democrats viewed as a key flip opportunity, Decision Desk HQ projects. Bennett led Kean 60.3 percent to 38.3 percent with 76 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 9:46 p.m.…
articles.body:
Former healthcare executive Rebecca Bennett will defeat Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R) in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District, capitalizing on what many Democrats viewed as a key flip opportunity, Decision Desk HQ projects .

Bennett led Kean 60.3 percent to 38.3 percent with 76 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 9:46 p.m. EST Tuesday.

The race was already seen as a strong pickup opportunity for Democrats, as President Trump carried the district by only 2 percentage points in 2024. But the race received much more attention and the incumbent garnered significant scrutiny over his months-long absence from the Capitol without explanation.

Kean’s absence began in March, and he didn’t return to Washington until the end of June. His office for months didn’t provide details of his situation and only indicated he was dealing with a health issue and would return soon. Kean’s GOP colleagues said they weren’t sure where he was or what he was dealing with.

The congressman eventually returned after an absence of four months, revealing he was being treated for depression. He said his doctors recommended he stay in the hospital, and what he believed would not be a long-term stay grew longer.

Kean’s explanation cleared up the confusion but not the scrutiny, as critics took issue with the significant amount of time that he spent away without any explanation given to his constituents.

Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot, didn’t focus much on Kean’s absence during the campaign, instead focusing on affordability concerns and tying the incumbent to the unpopular president.

Kean is the scion of a longtime New Jersey political family and the son of former Gov. Thomas Kean (R), who led the state in the 1980s. He flipped the seat in 2022 and narrowly won reelection in 2024 but fell short in his bid for a third term.

images.caption: Democratic congressional nominee Rebecca Bennett holds her daughter before casting her ballot at a Dropbox in Bridgewater, N.J., Oct. 26, 2026.

articles.title: Democrat J.D. Ford beats Spartz in major upset for Indiana House seat
articles.summary: Democrat J.D. Ford is projected to beat Rep. Victoria Spartz (R-Ind.), who represents a district President Trump won by 17 points in 2024, for a Republican-favored House seat, according to Decision Desk HQ. Ford, a state senator, ousted the Indiana Republican in the state’s 5th Congressional District, located northwest of Indianapolis. Ford’s victory shocked…
articles.body:
Democrat J.D. Ford is projected to beat Rep. Victoria Spartz (R-Ind.), who represents a district President Trump won by 17 points in 2024, for a Republican-favored House seat, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Ford, a state senator, ousted the Indiana Republican in the state’s 5th Congressional District, located northwest of Indianapolis. Ford’s victory shocked observers, given Spartz represents a reliably GOP district and wasn’t expected to be in play.

Ford’s victory portends serious warning signs for Republicans, who expected a good night for Democrats but thought they would eke wins in more reliably Republican districts.

The win is notable given that Trump and national Republicans pressured state lawmakers to redistrict and create an aggressive GOP gerrymander in the state that would have given the party a chance to pick up two more House seats.

Indiana currently has a 7-2 GOP edge in the House delegation. The new map would have created a 9-0 lean for the GOP, but Indiana Senate Republicans ultimately rebuffed those calls, angering the president.

In addition to being the first Democrat to hold the seat in more than three decades, Ford will be Indiana’s first openly gay member of Congress.

articles.title: Luria defeats Kiggans in rematch for Virginia House seat
articles.summary: Former Rep. Elaine Luria (D-Va.) is projected to beat GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans for Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). The two last faced off in 2024, when Kiggans challenged the Democratic representative for the seat she had held for two terms. DDHQ projected that Luria defeated Kiggans by 6 percentage…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Elaine Luria (D-Va.) is projected to beat GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans for Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

The two last faced off in 2024 , when Kiggans challenged the Democratic representative for the seat she had held for two terms.

DDHQ projected that Luria defeated Kiggans by 6 percentage points, with 73 percent of votes reported at 9:50 p.m. EST.

Kiggans has supported President Trump’s key policy objectives, including the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act.

Luria, meanwhile, has been a vocal critic of the president. She served as one of the original members on a House panel investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.

Trump won the district by less than a percentage point over former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, while Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) carried the district by 8 points in 2025.

A poll leading up to Election Day found that Luria held a slight lead to her opponent — 46 percent of likely voters in a Christopher Newport University poll said they would choose the Democrat, compared with 43 percent who said they would choose Kiggans. Ten percent were undecided, and 2 percent favored another candidate.

Campaign finance reports show that Luria raised more money than the incumbent, even in areas that have historically leaned red.

Both women are U.S. Navy veterans. Luria is also a small business owner.

Virginia’s 2nd District encompasses the Virginia Beach area, and it represents one of the largest military populations in the country.

articles.title: Democrats flip Nebraska’s ‘blue dot’ 2nd District
articles.summary: Democrat Denise Powell is projected to win the race for Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a pickup for Democrats in a key battleground district. Powell was leading Republican Brinker Harding by 20 percentage points — 59 percent to 39 percent — with 71 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ…
articles.body:
Democrat Denise Powell is projected to win the race for Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a pickup for Democrats in a key battleground district.

Powell was leading Republican Brinker Harding by 20 percentage points — 59 percent to 39 percent — with 71 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 9:51 p.m. EST.

Powell defeated Harding, an Omaha City Council member, and will fill the seat left open by Rep. Don Bacon’s (R) retirement.

Before launching her bid for Congress, Powell founded an organization to support local candidates across Nebraska. In her campaign, she hit the Trump administration for rising prices and the Trump family’s growing wealth, pledging to grow the economy and lower costs.

Harding was supported by President Trump and Bacon, though he did not promote Trump’s endorsement on his campaign website . Courier Nebraska noted that while Trump held a rally in Nebraska in the final weeks of the campaign, Harding did not attend .

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) campaigned for Harding over the summer , but as the House battlefield shifted toward redder seats, the district received less attention.

Powell was supported by a slew of national Democrats, including visits from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

The win marks a major step forward for Democrats in Nebraska’s 2nd District, who have for years been unable to flip the seat despite its blue lean nationally.

Nebraska splits its electoral votes in presidential elections by congressional district, and Nebraska’s 2nd has consistently been the most competitive of the state’s three districts. Democrats have carried the 2nd in the past two presidential elections, with former Vice President Kamala Harris winning the district by 4 points in 2024. Bacon won reelection on the same ballot by just less than 2 points.

The district was widely expected to flip to the Democrats, as Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball — two nonpartisan election forecasters — both rated the race “likely Democratic” in their final race ratings. DDHQ gave Powell more than a 90 percent chance to win ahead of the election.

Powell will be the first woman to represent the 2nd District.

articles.title: Darline Graham falls to Democrat Annie Andrews in stunning Senate GOP defeat
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.), whom President Trump personally picked to succeed her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and was then encouraged by the president to run for a full term, has been projected to be defeated by Democrat Annie Andrews in a stunning loss for the GOP, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).…
articles.body:
Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.), whom President Trump personally picked to succeed her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and was then encouraged by the president to run for a full term, has been projected to be defeated by Democrat Annie Andrews in a stunning loss for the GOP, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Andrews leads Graham by 4 points with 84 percent reporting, according to DDHQ.

Graham’s loss, projected by Decision Desk HQ, moves the Senate closer to Democratic control, and gives the party a victory few would have seen coming just a month ago. At the beginning of the year, before Lindsey Graham’s death, it would have been nearly inconceivable.

The race had been edging closer and closer for weeks, with polls showing Andrews with a lead going into Election Day. Still, DDHQ, among other prognosticators, had Darline Graham as the favorite Tuesday.

But Darline Graham trailed badly in her vote totals behind what her brother had won in the state, after a rocky campaign that saw her win a tough primary battle over Rep. Ralph Norman.

She stumbled in one primary debate on foreign policy while taking a question on Taiwan, a moment that raised concerns among Republicans about her readiness for the race.

Lindsey Graham died unexpectedly in July after serving in the upper chamber since the early 2000s and after winning an initial June primary as he tried for a fifth Senate term.

Darline Graham was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) to temporarily fill the vacancy, marking the first time a sibling has been sworn in to replace a senator who died in office. She later launched a bid for a full term with Trump’s support and defeated Norman in a bitter primary runoff .

The Republican had the advantage in red South Carolina, but Cook Political Report shifted the race toward Democrats in the weeks ahead of the election, citing Graham’s political weaknesses and a competitive bid from Andrews, a pediatrician and political newcomer.

A Libertarian on the ballot, Kasie Whitener, also risked pulling some of Graham’s support to create a path for Andrews .

Norman’s son, Warren Norman, said ahead of the election that he would not vote for Graham and was “leaning” toward casting his ballot for Andrews .

A bipartisan pair of former South Carolina governors, David Beasley (R) and Jim Hodges (D), also endorsed Andrews just more than a week before Election Day.

“Now, over the years, the two of us haven’t always agreed on everything,” Hodges said.

“But one thing we do agree on right now is this country is too divided, and the political rhetoric has gotten way, way out of hand,” Beasley stated.

The results are a blow to Trump, who has said he recommended the late senator’s sister as an interim replacement, and he later called on her to run for a full term. As she campaigned, Graham touted her alignment with the president as she batted back criticisms about her lack of political experience.

Trump stumped for Graham and other Republicans in the Palmetto State in the closing days of the campaign.

Graham was close with her brother and a key fixture in his political life, though she had never held political office before her Senate appointment. Andrews’s win ends her tenure as the first woman and first graduate from a historically Black college or university to represent South Carolina in the Senate.

Both of South Carolina’s Senate seats have been red for decades, and Republicans dominate the state’s House seats and presidential races.

articles.title: Sand flips Iowa governor’s mansion in major win for Democrats
articles.summary: Democrat Rob Sand is projected to win the race for Iowa governor, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Despite the state heavily favoring Republicans in recent years — President Trump won Iowa by more than 13 percentage points in 2024 — Sand was leading his GOP opponent, Zach Lahn, in the polls ahead of Election…
articles.body:
Democrat Rob Sand is projected to win the race for Iowa governor, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Despite the state heavily favoring Republicans in recent years — President Trump won Iowa by more than 13 percentage points in 2024 — Sand was leading his GOP opponent, Zach Lahn, in the polls ahead of Election Day for the open seat. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) opted not to seek a third term.

DDHQ projected Sand won over Lahn by about 23 percentage points with 26 percent of votes reported as of 9:57 p.m. EST.

Sand is the first Democrat to win the Iowa governor’s office in nearly 20 years, and he has a reputation as a political survivor. Sand was the only Democrat to win a statewide race when he was reelected as state auditor in 2022.

Despite the Democratic label, Sand presented himself on the campaign trail as a centrist who would rather be unaligned with either party.

Sand and Lahn both leaned into the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) movement, blaming “Big Ag” for Iowa’s cancer rates and supporting expanded conservation efforts to reduce pollution in waterways.

Still, Sand’s victory is a blow to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s vision of MAHA as an arm of the Republican Party, closely aligned with Trump and MAGA.

Republicans banked on Kennedy and the MAHA label being enough to boost turnout for the GOP, even though MAHA isn’t always aligned with traditional Republican views.

articles.title: Alan Wilson wins South Carolina governor’s race
articles.summary: South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson (R) is projected to defeat Democratic state Rep. Jermaine Johnson in the state’s governor’s race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Wilson, who has served as the Palmetto State’s top prosecutor since 2011, will succeed term-limited Gov. Henry McMaster (R), extending the GOP’s control of the governor’s mansion. Wilson…
articles.body:
South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson (R) is projected to defeat Democratic state Rep. Jermaine Johnson in the state’s governor’s race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Wilson, who has served as the Palmetto State’s top prosecutor since 2011, will succeed term-limited Gov. Henry McMaster (R), extending the GOP’s control of the governor’s mansion.

Wilson led Johnson by nearly 7 percentage points with 84 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 9:54 p.m. Tuesday.

The Republican emerged from a crowded gubernatorial primary that included South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette and GOP Reps. Nancy Mace and Ralph Norman.

Wilson initially finished second to Evette in the June primary but defeated her in a runoff later that month, winning approximately 69 percent of the vote.

President Trump initially endorsed Evette but later backed both candidates ahead of the runoff. Wilson also received endorsements from GOP Sens. Tim Scott (S.C.) and Ted Cruz (Texas).

DDHQ gave the Republican a 77 percent chance of winning heading into Election Day.

Wilson campaigned on lowering taxes, cutting government spending and improving infrastructure. He proposed eliminating South Carolina’s state income tax and conducting audits of state agencies to identify wasteful spending.

Johnson, a state lawmaker representing the Columbia, S.C., area, campaigned on raising wages, expanding access to healthcare and making housing more affordable.

The two candidates sparred over taxes and Medicaid during an October debate . Wilson opposed expanding the healthcare assistance, citing concerns about the state’s ability to afford the program, while Johnson supported a proposed expansion.

Wilson, a colonel in the South Carolina Army National Guard, was first elected to his role as top prosecutor in 2010 and became the longest-serving attorney general in state history.

Republicans have controlled the governor’s mansion in the state since 2003, when former Gov. Mark Sanford (R) took office. The state last elected a Democratic governor in 1998.

images.caption: Alan Wilson, Republican nominee for governor of South Carolina, speaks at a campaign rally in Rock Hill, S.C., Oct. 29, 2026.

articles.title: Gonzalez defends battleground House seat in Texas
articles.summary: Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez is projected to win reelection in Texas’s 34th District, defeating GOP challenger Eric Flores to defend the battleground seat, according to Decision Desk HQ. The South Texas lawmaker was first elected to the House in 2016, serving three terms representing Texas’s 15th District before winning the 2022 race for the state’s…
articles.body:
Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez is projected to win reelection in Texas’s 34th District, defeating GOP challenger Eric Flores to defend the battleground seat, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The South Texas lawmaker was first elected to the House in 2016, serving three terms representing Texas’s 15th District before winning the 2022 race for the state’s 34th District.

The moderate Democrat served on the House Financial Services Committee and has introduced bipartisan legislation aimed at supporting the state’s oil and gas industries and to increase transparency around military funding.

The Democrat campaigned on lowering living costs, safeguarding benefits for seniors and veterans, protecting women’s rights, and expanding access to healthcare and education.

The 34th District runs along a stretch of Texas’s border with Mexico and covers part of the Rio Grande Valley, including a portion of Corpus Christi and the border city of Brownsville.

The district — which was redrawn in the GOP’s favor in 2025 during a mid-decade redistricting push led by state Republicans — includes a large Latino population and is considered a swing district. Just a little more than 50 percent of voters in this district supported former President Biden in the 2020 presidential election, while nearly 55 percent backed President Trump in the 2024 race.

Flores, the Republican nominee in this race and a U.S. Army veteran, put up a competitive fight after handily winning the state’s GOP primary election. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, rated the November race as a “toss-up.”

The incumbent lawmaker’s victory marks a win for House Democrats as they fight to regain their majority in the lower legislative chamber.

articles.title: Former House Democrat wins Utah election to return to Capitol Hill
articles.summary: Former Rep. Ben McAdams (D) is projected to win the race to represent Utah’s 1st Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ. The Democrat defeated Republican nominee Riley Owen in the election to replace GOP Rep. Blake Moore, who opted to run in the state’s 2nd District after his seat was redrawn in Democrats’ favor.…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Ben McAdams (D) is projected to win the race to represent Utah’s 1st Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The Democrat defeated Republican nominee Riley Owen in the election to replace GOP Rep. Blake Moore, who opted to run in the state’s 2nd District after his seat was redrawn in Democrats’ favor.

DDHQ projected the race for McAdams at 10 p.m. EST.

McAdams previously represented Utah’s 4th District from 2019 to 2021, serving as the only Democratic member of Utah’s congressional delegation during this time period. He lost his seat in 2020 to Rep. Burgess Owens (R).

The moderate Democrat campaigned on reducing everyday costs, protecting public lands, defending human rights and increasing accountability and oversight of President Trump’s immigration enforcement operations.

Prior to his time in government, the Democrat worked as a lawyer in Salt Lake City and served as a senior adviser to former city Mayor Ralph Becker (D).

His campaign garnered support from the Human Rights Campaign , the American Federation of Government Employees, Moms Demand Action, Defend the Vote, and New Democrat Coalition Action Fund.

articles.title: White House blames bad GOP candidates as poor results come in for Republicans
articles.summary: The White House laid blame on Republican candidates as poor results for the GOP rolled in on election night. In a statement on Tuesday evening, a White House official described the mood inside the White House as “defiant.” “President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he…
articles.body:
The White House laid blame on Republican candidates as poor results for the GOP rolled in on election night.

In a statement on Tuesday evening, a White House official described the mood inside the White House as “defiant.”

“President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot,” the official said.

“Also, candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves,” the official added.

The statement came as Republicans faced a slew of losses on election night. Decision Desk HQ projected that Democrats will retake the House majority. Additionally, it projected that Democrats won Senate seats in Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina. Early returns out of Texas also showed tight races in the traditionally red state.

Trump spent much of the past month crisscrossing the country seeking to boost Republican candidates and urged his supporters to “pretend” he was on the ballot.

The latest statement from the White House is the first attempt to find a scapegoat for poor Republican midterm performances.

The White House official said voters who backed Democrats on Tuesday will regret their choice.

“Anyone who voted Democrat today is going to have a serious case of buyers remorse when gas prices come down quickly when the Iran conflict is solved but they’re still stuck with list of liberal extremist Democrats,” the official said. “And a final note here: regardless of how today plays out, President Trump’s resolve to stop the Radical Left is only going to become stronger. Buckle up.”

articles.body:
Rep. Barry Moore (R-Ala.) is projected to win the race to succeed Alabama GOP Sen. Tommy Tuberville, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Tuberville, a former college football coach, decided to exit the upper chamber after one term to run for Alabama governor.

The result is also a victory for President Trump, who backed Moore in the race to keep the Senate seat in the deep-red Cotton State in Republican hands. The president won Alabama by 30 percentage points in 2024.

In a Senate campaign announcement video , Moore touted being the first elected official in the country to endorse Trump for president in 2015, saying he “didn’t wait to see which way the wind was blowing.”

Moore, a member of the House Freedom Caucus, served three terms in the House and was previously in the U.S. Army National Guard. He became the Republican nominee after defeating U.S. Navy SEAL Jared Hudson in a June runoff .

Moore had been all but certain to defeat Democrat Everett Weiss, an attorney who won a runoff himself . The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rated the Alabama Senate seat as “solid Republican.”

articles.title: Sen. Mike Rounds wins reelection in South Dakota
articles.summary: GOP Sen. Mike Rounds is projected to win reelection in South Dakota’s Senate race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Rounds was expected to defeat his opponent, Democrat-turned-Independent Brian Bengs, in the reliably Republican state. Bengs was not well-funded, and a previous Democratic challenger withdrew in August. The incumbent, 72, has served in the Senate…
articles.body:
GOP Sen. Mike Rounds is projected to win reelection in South Dakota’s Senate race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Rounds was expected to defeat his opponent, Democrat-turned-Independent Brian Bengs, in the reliably Republican state. Bengs was not well-funded, and a previous Democratic challenger withdrew in August .

The incumbent, 72, has served in the Senate since 2015 after a stint as the Mount Rushmore State’s governor from 2003 to 2011.

The senator is a moderate Republican who has not always backed President Trump, but he carried his endorsement this year.

In the Senate, he sits on the Appropriations, Armed Services, Banking, Indian Affairs and Intelligence committees, often putting him in the center of negotiations over foreign policy and government funding. He also chairs the Senate Artificial Intelligence Caucus and a related bipartisan working group focused on AI policy.

Rounds was a key driver of the bipartisan housing package that passed both chambers earlier this year and has worked on provisions in the annual defense policy bill to support Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota.

DDHQ gave the incumbent a 95 percent chance of winning reelection heading into Election Day.

articles.summary: Democrat JoAnna Mendoza is the projected winner of Arizona’s heavily contested 6th Congressional District, defeating incumbent Rep. Juan Ciscomani (R), according to Decision Desk HQ. Ahead of Election Day, Ciscomani’s seat was considered one of Democrats’ most competitive races in their quest to flip control of the House.
