articles.body:
Democrat JoAnna Mendoza is the projected winner of Arizona’s heavily contested 6th Congressional District, defeating incumbent Rep. Juan Ciscomani (R), according to Decision Desk HQ.

Ahead of Election Day, Ciscomani’s seat was considered one of Democrats’ most competitive races in their quest to flip control of the House. The party needs a net gain of three seats to retake the lower chamber.

DDHQ projected that Mendoza defeated Ciscomani by 18.5 percentage points with 70 percent of the race called at 10:13 p.m. EST Tuesday.

Ciscomani was first elected in 2022 and narrowly won reelection, but Democrats have carried the district in statewide races.

Mendoza is a 20-year veteran of the Navy and Marine Corps. Her campaign focused heavily on Ciscomani’s consistent support for GOP policies she argued made life more expensive for the district’s constituents — like the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the GOP’s signature legislation that will cut close to $1 trillion from Medicaid and more than $180 billion from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.

images.caption: JoAnna Mendoza (D), left, an Arizona Congressional District 6 candidate, talks with a campaign volunteer before a weekly neighborhood canvass, Oct. 15, 2026, in Oro Valley, Ariz.

articles.title: Talarico turns Texas blue in historic win for Democrats
articles.summary: Democrat James Talarico is projected to win a Senate seat in Texas, defeating Republican Ken Paxton and delivering his party its first big Lone Star state win in decades, according to a projection by Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). It’s a huge moment for Democrats, both because it finally notches the party a big victory in…
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico is projected to win a Senate seat in Texas, defeating Republican Ken Paxton and delivering his party its first big Lone Star state win in decades, according to a projection by Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

It’s a huge moment for Democrats, both because it finally notches the party a big victory in a state key to presidential elections and because it edges them closer to winning a Senate majority.

The party needs to net four seats to take back the majority, and at the beginning of the year, a win in Texas seemed like a long shot.

It is also a huge blow to Republicans in general, and specifically to President Trump, who endorsed controversial Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in a contentious GOP primary runoff.

Many Republicans saw Cornyn as the much safer pick and will believe that in endorsing Paxton, who easily defeated Cornyn in a primary after the endorsement, the president helped deliver a historic victory to Democrats.

Talarico, the 37-year-old state lawmaker, was seen as Democrats’ best chance in years to break through the GOP’s domination of statewide seats.

Talarico’s measured bid focused on a unity message, leaning into his faith and experience as a Presbyterian seminarian and former public school teacher. He was one of the Democratic state legislators who fled Texas last year in a bid to stall GOP-friendly redistricting and drew comparisons to Democrat Beto O’Rourke, who came within a few points of ousting Sen. Ted Cruz (R) in 2018.

Ahead of Election Day, the Democrat narrowly led in DDHQ’s polling averages, and forecasts signaled he was slightly favored to pull i off after raising a staggering $64 million in the third quarter of the year, compared to Paxton’s $18 million .

But a number of Democrats, who had seen previous efforts to win in Texas fall short, were not ready to believe their party could win the Senate seat until actually seeing it.

Paxton was a controversial Senate pick because of a long history of scandals. As the state’s top attorney, he faced criticism of politicizing the office and an unsuccessful 2023 impeachment on corruption charges. His wife of nearly four decades filed for divorce last year on “biblical grounds.”

As he struggled to gain on Talarico in polls ahead of the election, Paxton was a focal point during the Republican National Committee’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas but later said that the convention “dropped our numbers,” according to audio leaked by The New York Times in September.

Trump, whose own approval rating has been dragged down by frustration over the economy and the war in Iran, offered a somewhat reticent pitch for Paxton during his campaign trail speeches, saying that Paxton was “a pain in the a‑‑” and “a little controversial,” even as he called on Texans to vote for the Republican.

Meanwhile, Republicans worked to paint Talarico as too progressive , pointing to controversial past remarks that the Democrat has since sought to clarify.

But it wasn’t enough to hold on to the seat that Cornyn easily won each cycle since 2002 .

The rivals never faced off on a debate stage, though Talarico and Trump both called for one.

The Texas contest was one of the most expensive of the cycle. Trump’s MAGA Inc. dropped $10 million into the race in early September, and tech mogul Elon Musk poured $158 million into a key super PAC backing Paxton, according to filings ahead of the election.

Talarico accused Musk in October of trying to “ buy his own personal U.S. senator. ”

The Democrat, though, won with some notable support from GOP figures who could not bring themselves to cast a ballot for Paxton, including former President George W. Bush’s brother, Neil, and personal injury lawyer Thomas J. Henry , a former Paxton donor.

images.caption: Texas state Rep. James Talarico speaks for the first time since winning the Democratic nomination in Austin, March 4, 2026.

articles.title: Democrats hold Arizona governor’s mansion with Hobbs win
articles.summary: Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs (D) is projected to maintain the purple state’s gubernatorial mansion, per Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). The Democrat fended off a challenge from Republican Rep. Andy Biggs (Ariz.) to clinch a second term leading the Grand Canyon State. She led her opponent in the polls heading into Election Day, with DDHQ and…
articles.body:
Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs (D) is projected to maintain the purple state’s gubernatorial mansion, per Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

The Democrat fended off a challenge from Republican Rep. Andy Biggs (Ariz.) to clinch a second term leading the Grand Canyon State. She led her opponent in the polls heading into Election Day, with DDHQ and Cook Political Report forecasting the race as leaning in Democrats’ favor.

An Arizona governor has not lost reelection since 1967.

The state’s last gubernatorial contest garnered national headlines after Hobbs’s opponent, Republican Kari Lake, filed the highest-profile election case challenging the 2022 results and refused to concede. The lawsuits were all ultimately dismissed .

Hobbs refused to debate Biggs on the campaign trail, with her campaign telling the Arizona Mirror that “face-to-face engagement with Arizonans is more effective than a stage designed for short soundbites and political theater.” The Democrat also declined to debate Lake in 2022.

Biggs, a staunch ally of President Trump, fiscal hawk and member of the House Freedom Caucus , voted to overturn the 2020 election results and alleged widespread fraud in Arizona’s contest.

Republicans currently control both the state House and Senate, but both majorities are on the line Tuesday. Hobbs has set the state’s veto record — 541 since 2023, per the Mirror.

The governor chose a former GOP mayor as her running mate in the purple state that voted for Trump twice and former President Biden in 2020.

Prior to the governorship, Hobbs, a social worker, served as Arizona secretary of State from 2019 to 2023 after an eight-year stint in the State Legislature.

images.caption: Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs smiles as she meets with campaign volunteers as voters cast their ballots on primary election day, on July 21, 2026, in Phoenix.

articles.title: Weiser wins Colorado governor race, succeeding Polis
articles.summary: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser (D) will win his election to be the state’s next governor, Decision Desk HQ projects. Weiser’s victory seemed all but assured in the Democratic stronghold against Republican Victor Marx, a ministry leader. Weiser will succeed outgoing Gov. Jared Polis (D), who is term-limited. With nearly half of the ballots counted, Weiser…
articles.body:
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser (D) will win his election to be the state’s next governor, Decision Desk HQ projects .

Weiser’s victory seemed all but assured in the Democratic stronghold against Republican Victor Marx, a ministry leader. Weiser will succeed outgoing Gov. Jared Polis (D), who is term-limited.

With nearly half of the ballots counted, Weiser had just more than 64 percent of the vote.

Beyond Colorado’s increasing shift to the left in recent years, Weiser was viewed as the favorite particularly because of controversies surrounding his opponent.

Marx drew attention and scrutiny during his campaign for various past comments he made, including that his stepfather once forced him to kill a man when he was 7 years old. In an eyebrow-raising interview in May, Marx said he couldn’t say whether he had killed other people as an adult.

Marx also faced scrutiny over the accuracy of past statements his campaign has asserted about how many women and children he’s helped save through missions. Several high-profile Republicans refused to endorse Marx, including both of his primary opponents.

President Trump hasn’t included Marx on his extensive list of endorsements he’s made for fellow Republicans. Former GOP Rep. Ken Buck (Colo.), a former state party chair, even endorsed Weiser.

Weiser will become the second Jewish governor of Colorado, following Polis. This will also mark the first time in U.S. history that a Jewish governor of a state is succeeded by another Jewish governor.

images.caption: Phil Weiser, Democratic candidate for Colorado governor, talks during a rally at the carpenters’ union headquarters before members set out to canvass for the candidate Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026, in northeast Denver. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski)

articles.title: Robert White wins DC’s non-voting House seat
articles.summary: D.C. City Council Member Robert White is projected to win the race to be the District’s next delegate to the House of Representatives, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). White will take over for longtime Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.) as a non-voting delegate in the House. He beat Republican Denise Rosado and Green Party…
articles.body:
D.C. City Council Member Robert White is projected to win the race to be the District’s next delegate to the House of Representatives, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

White will take over for longtime Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.) as a non-voting delegate in the House. He beat Republican Denise Rosado and Green Party candidate Kymone Freeman for what was widely viewed as a safely Democratic seat.

DDHQ projected that White defeated Rosado by 81.3 percentage points with 71 percent of the vote reported as of 10:16 p.m. EST.

White ran on defending the District from President Trump’s efforts to inflict control over the city, safeguarding the municipal budget and pushing back on any effort to diminish D.C.’s self-governing, home rule status.

“Together, we will fight Trump and his allies in Congress as they attempt to use D.C. as a testing ground for their radical right-wing agenda,” White says on his campaign website .

White also pledged to fight for affordable housing and access to health care, childcare and well-paying jobs. The councilman said he would continue the fight for D.C. statehood, a cause long elevated by Homes Norton.

“D.C. is not asking America to save us,” White’s website says. “Give us the voice, freedom, and power we have earned, and Washingtonians will help lead America forward.”

images.caption: Robert White Jr., a District of Columbia Council member, speaks during a D.C. Council hearing regarding the fiscal 2027 budget at the Wilson Building, City Hall on June 9, 2026, in Washington.

articles.title: Crowley wins Wisconsin governor’s race to succeed Evers
articles.summary: Democrat David Crowley is projected to defeat Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in the Wisconsin governor’s race, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Crowley was leading 54 percent to 46 percent with 63 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 10:20 p.m. EST. Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, will fill the…
articles.body:
Democrat David Crowley is projected to defeat Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in the Wisconsin governor’s race, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Crowley was leading 54 percent to 46 percent with 63 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 10:20 p.m. EST.

Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, will fill the seat of retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, who endorsed him in the state’s Democratic primary.

The 40-year-old Wisconsin native was the youngest person to be named county executive in Milwaukee County history, and he was the first Black person to hold the office when he stepped into the role in May 2020.

Now, Crowley is Wisconsin’s first Black governor.

President Trump won Wisconsin in the last presidential election, but it has become a swing state in the past decade.

Crowley notably defeated progressive Francesca Hong in the Badger State’s Democratic primary in August , despite trailing by double-digits in polling.

He originally exited the race in early July, placing his support behind Wisconsin Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez but eventually rejoined the campaign trail once Rodriguez dropped out in mid-July.

After Crowley’s upset victory over Hong, election handicapper Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted November’s general election toward Democrats. DDHQ listed the race as “leans Democrat.”

Crowley grew up in Milwaukee and enrolled at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee to study community engagement and education, but he did not complete his degree due to political work. He ultimately earned his degree 20 years later in 2024.

images.caption: Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley stands before a debate against Republican nominee Tom Tiffany at Marquette University Law School, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, in Milwaukee. (AP Photo/Lizzy Larson)

articles.title: Vasquez defends New Mexico House seat
articles.summary: Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D) fended off a tough challenge in New Mexico’s 2nd District on Tuesday, securing a third term and frustrating Republicans who have seen the seat as a top pick-up opportunity for several cycles, Decision Desk HQ projects. Vasquez defeated GOP challenger Greg Cunningham, a Marine veteran and retired Albuquerque police detective who…
articles.body:
Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D) fended off a tough challenge in New Mexico’s 2nd District on Tuesday, securing a third term and frustrating Republicans who have seen the seat as a top pick-up opportunity for several cycles, Decision Desk HQ projects.

Vasquez defeated GOP challenger Greg Cunningham, a Marine veteran and retired Albuquerque police detective who ran on a platform of secure borders and tough law enforcement.

DDHQ projected that Vasquez beat Cunningham by 17.5 percent with 40 percent of votes counted as of 10:23 p.m. EST.

Republicans hoped that message would resonate in the 2nd District, a massive region that runs the entire length of New Mexico’s border with Mexico. President Trump had carried the district by 2 percentage points in 2024.

But the political environment this year is much different than it was just two years ago, as voters have soured on Trump amid an unpopular Iran war, a volatile economy and a cost-of-living crisis that’s seen the price of numerous consumer goods — including staples like gas, groceries and housing — increase under the president’s watch.

Those trends have been a drag on GOP candidates across the country. And Cunningham was challenged further by Trump’s aggressive deportation surge, which has led to the capture and expulsion of violent criminals, but also resulted in the killings of U.S. citizens and unarmed immigrants living in the country legally.

That issue has resonated throughout the country but carries a special significance in a Hispanic-heavy border district like New Mexico’s 2nd. Indeed, heading into Tuesday, polls showed that the gains Trump had made with Hispanic voters in 2024 had been erased this cycle, largely because of his aggressive immigration enforcement agenda.

On one issue, the two candidates found agreement: Both Vasquez and Cunningham opposed Trump’s push to rename their state “New America.”

“I’m a proud New Mexican,”Cunningham said during a debate last month , “and that’s what we’re going to stay.”

images.caption: Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) speaks during a news conference to introduce newly elected members of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus on Capitol Hill, Nov. 15, 2024, in Washington.

articles.title: Duffy’s son-in-law wins Wisconsin House seat
articles.summary: Michael Alfonso (R), the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, is projected to win Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ. The 26-year-old is set to be the youngest member of Congress, succeeding outgoing Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.), who placed a gubernatorial bid this midterm cycle. Alfonso faced off against Fred Clark, a…
articles.body:
Michael Alfonso (R), the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, is projected to win Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The 26-year-old is set to be the youngest member of Congress, succeeding outgoing Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.), who placed a gubernatorial bid this midterm cycle.

Alfonso faced off against Fred Clark, a former Democratic state representative. The GOP candidate was bolstered by endorsements from President Trump and Duffy.

The Republican led his challenger by almost 11 percentage points — 55.3 to 44.7 percent — with 57 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 10:25 p.m. Tuesday.

The Transportation secretary praised his son-in-law’s past experience working in construction in the district.

“I think it’d be great to have someone who knows how to put on a pair of jeans and a pair of boots and a hard hat and work his butt off 12 hours a day,” Duffy said in an August interview on NewsNation’s “Morning in America.”

The president called Alfonso a “MAGA warrior” and a “young ‘STAR” in May.

Alfonso ran his campaign close to Trump. He said on social media that receiving the president’s endorsement was the “greatest honor.” His campaign focused on affordability and personal freedoms, while emphasizing the need for a new generation of Republican leaders.

“We need to have young Republicans who can actually go out and message to these young people and talk about the issues they care about — affordability, owning homes, raising families,” Alfonso told NewsNation in the same interview as his father-in-law. “That’s what I’m doing.”

Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District is made up of northwestern and central parts of the state. It leans red.

images.caption: Michael Alfonso, the GOP candidate running for election in the House to represent Wisconsin’s 7th District, speaks during a campaign event on Aug. 4, 2026, in New Richmond, Wis.

articles.title: Taylor ousts Wittman from Virginia’s 1st District in Democratic win
articles.summary: Democrat Shannon Taylor, a longtime Virginia prosecutor, is projected to unseat Rep. Rob Wittman (R-Va.) in Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ, with Taylor ousting a Republican incumbent who has held the seat for nearly two decades. Taylor, the commonwealth’s attorney for Henrico County, defeated the 10-term incumbent in a district that…
articles.body:
Democrat Shannon Taylor, a longtime Virginia prosecutor, is projected to unseat Rep. Rob Wittman (R-Va.) in Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ, with Taylor ousting a Republican incumbent who has held the seat for nearly two decades.

Taylor, the commonwealth’s attorney for Henrico County, defeated the 10-term incumbent in a district that had long been considered a Republican stronghold but grew increasingly competitive in the months leading up to the midterm elections.

Wittman first won the seat in a 2007 special election and had not faced a serious reelection challenge until this year. He defeated Democrat Leslie Mehta by nearly 13 percentage points in 2024, while President Trump won the district by roughly 5 points that year.

The district, which stretches from the Richmond suburbs to the Northern Neck and Middle Peninsula, has become more competitive as suburban voters have shifted toward Democrats.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report moved the race from “lean Republican” to “toss-up” in October, citing troubling trends for the longtime incumbent and a difficult political environment for Republicans.

Taylor emerged as the Democratic nominee from a crowded seven-way primary in August with 53 percent of the vote, defeating Salaam Bhatti and five other candidates. Taylor also secured the backing of Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) and Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.).

She also benefited from a significant advantage in outside spending. While Wittman spent more on his own television advertising — outspending Taylor $2.2 million to $1.6 million through October — Democratic groups including the House Majority PAC and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee poured money into the race to support Taylor. Wittman received comparatively less outside support from national Republicans.

Democrats sought to attack Wittman by highlighting his history of stock trading while serving in Congress, making the issue a central focus of their advertisements against the Republican incumbent.

Wittman, meanwhile, attacked Taylor’s record as a prosecutor, questioning her handling of criminal cases during her tenure as the commonwealth’s attorney for Henrico County.

Taylor has held that position since 2012, after previously serving as a prosecutor in Richmond. She highlighted her law enforcement experience throughout her campaign, including her role in prosecuting former Virginia state Sen. Joseph Morrissey (D) as evidence that she was willing to hold members of both parties accountable.

images.caption: Congressional candidate Shannon Taylor, D-Va., speaks during a campaign rally, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026, in Henrico, Va. (AP Photo/Mike Kropf)

articles.title: Pingree wins Maine governor’s race
articles.summary: Former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree (D) was projected to defeat Republican Bobby Charles in the state’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), with Pingree securing a third consecutive term for Democrats. Pingree will succeed outgoing Democratic Gov. Janet Mills, who is term limited. She faced Charles, a former George W. Bush administration…
articles.body:
Former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree (D) was projected to defeat Republican Bobby Charles in the state’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), with Pingree securing a third consecutive term for Democrats.

Pingree will succeed outgoing Democratic Gov. Janet Mills, who is term limited. She faced Charles, a former George W. Bush administration official, as well as independent candidate Rick Bennett, a former Republican state Senate president.

DDHQ projected that Pingree defeated Charles by almost 6 percentage points with 29 percent of the vote counted as of 10:32 p.m. EST.

Pingree, daughter of Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), has a long legislative history in the state. She was first elected to the Maine House in 2002 at age 26, later rising to House majority leader and then House Speaker by age 32, becoming the second woman to serve in that role.

She left the state Legislature in 2010 because of term limits, later leading the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future under Mills.

Hannah Pingree emerged from a crowded Democratic primary that included former Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention Director Nirav Shah, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, former clean energy executive Angus King III and former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, who went on to replace Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate this cycle.

Pingree initially trailed Shah in first-choice votes but won the ranked-choice count on the fourth round, drawing support from voters whose preferred candidates were eliminated.

Pingree entered the final days of the race as the favorite, even as Jackson and Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) were locked in a competitive Senate contest. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated the race “Solid Democrat,” while DDHQ rated the race as “Likely Democrat” and gave Pingree an 85 percent chance of winning the race as of Friday.

images.caption: Democratic nominee for Maine Governor Hannah Pingree addresses supporters and potential voteers during a meet and greet for Democratic Maine Senate candidate Troy Jackson at the Maine Beer Company in Freeport, Maine, on Tuesday, October 27, 2026

articles.title: Acton defeats Ramaswamy in Ohio governor’s race
articles.summary: Democrat Amy Acton is projected to flip the Ohio governor’s mansion, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), after a controversial ad from Republican rival Vivek Ramaswamy roiled the closing days of the race. Acton was leading by 4 percentage points — 50 percent to 46 percent — with 76 percent of the vote reported by…
articles.body:
Democrat Amy Acton is projected to flip the Ohio governor’s mansion, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), after a controversial ad from Republican rival Vivek Ramaswamy roiled the closing days of the race.

Acton was leading by 4 percentage points — 50 percent to 46 percent — with 76 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 10:30 p.m. EST.

Acton is the first Democrat elected to the office in roughly 15 years, and the first woman elected as governor in Buckeye State history.

She’ll replace term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine (R), whose administration she worked with as a former director of the Ohio Department of Health.

Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur and billionaire who ran for president in 2024, boasted key endorsements from President Trump and Vice President Vance, who rallied in Ohio as part of their blitz through red states ahead of the election. But Acton held a slight lead in the polls as Election Day approached, and she may have gotten a boost from Ramaswamy’s contentious attack ad.

Ramaswamy put $4 million behind an ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother calling the Democrat “a liar,” though Acton described a childhood of abuse that culminated in rape charges against her late stepfather.

Trump and Vance came to Ramaswamy’s defense, but other figures on both sides of the aisle decried the ad. DeWine, who had endorsed Ramaswamy, called it “deeply, deeply troubling.” And Sen. Jon Husted (R), locked in a tough fight with former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D), said he “ would not have run ” the ad.

The ad was seen by many as a last-ditch attempt from Ramaswamy to make a splash among Ohio voters as he trailed Acton in polls, though experts expected it would backfire. Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the race out of the “toss-up” column to “lean Democratic” amid the fallout, calling it “not the kind of TV ad you run if you’re winning — or even if you’re confident you can.”

Ramaswamy, who founded the biotech company Roivant in 2014, poured millions into his White House bid in 2024 before dropping out to endorse Trump. He put an estimated $36 million of his own funds into the 2026 governor’s race as his campaign outspent Acton’s.

Acton, a physician, painted Ramaswamy as an out-of-touch billionaire and refused to debate him as the race ramped up. Her campaign said a showdown would be akin to “platforming a scam artist.”

Her win is a rare flip in Ohio, where the governor’s mansion has been red since 2010 — and where Trump won in each of his three presidential races, after the state swung blue for former President Obama’s two elections.

images.caption: Amy Acton, Democratic candidate for governor of Ohio, speaks at a campaign rally in Cleveland on Oct. 24, 2026.

articles.title: Cotton wins third term in Senate for Arkansas
articles.summary: Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) won his reelection campaign in Arkansas, securing a third term in the Senate, according to Decision Desk HQ. The outcome comes after many polls predicted Cotton would overcome his opponent, Democrat Hallie Shoffner. One poll from Hendrix College did turn some heads after it put Shoffner ahead in the deep-red state, but…
articles.body:
Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) won his reelection campaign in Arkansas, securing a third term in the Senate, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The outcome comes after many polls predicted Cotton would overcome his opponent, Democrat Hallie Shoffner.

One poll from Hendrix College did turn some heads after it put Shoffner ahead in the deep-red state, but the sixth-generation Arkansas farmer was not able to prevail.

Despite the race being labeled as “safe” for the Republican by Decision Desk HQ, Cotton vastly outspent his opponent by millions of dollars.

Cotton was first elected to the Senate in 2015 after previously serving in the military.

He has worked his way up in the Senate to the No. 3 position among Republicans and serves as chair of the Select Committee on Intelligence.

Cotton is known for his tough stance on illegal immigration and pushing for tax cuts, and he has generally aligned himself with the president.

Cotton and President Trump had a battle during the senator’s time on the campaign trail due to Cotton’s opposition to permanent daylight saving time , which Trump has strongly advocated for.

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton posted on social media. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”

images.caption: Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) leaves a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and senators to discuss the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 28, 2026.

articles.title: Hannity: Election results would have been ‘100 percent’ different without Iran war
articles.summary: Fox News host Sean Hannity conceded the U.S. war with Iran was a major factor driving the GOP’s sweeping losses in this week’s midterm elections. “I think 100 percent, I don’t think there’s any doubt about it,” Hannity said Tuesday when asked by Fox anchor Bret Baier if the Iran war had not been top…
articles.body:
Fox News host Sean Hannity conceded the U.S. war with Iran was a major factor driving the GOP’s sweeping losses in this week’s midterm elections.

“I think 100 percent, I don’t think there’s any doubt about it,” Hannity said Tuesday when asked by Fox anchor Bret Baier if the Iran war had not been top of mind for voters in this cycle would the results be different.

The Trump-supporting host maintained that while “fundamentals of the economy” are solid under the current administration, “if people don’t feel it, it is a problem.”

“The two years of any presidency is an incomplete grade,” Hannity continued. “People want to border secure, but they didn’t like a lot of the videos [of U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations] that were being hyped up by Democrats.”

Displeasure with the war with Iran and its impact on the economy “is the more dominant feeling force now,” Hannity added.

One of Fox’s longest serving hosts, Hannity has been vocally supportive of the president for years and hosted him for an exclusive interview Monday, just 24 hours before Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The president spent much of election night posting on Truth Social to complain about Fox’s coverage of the midterms, arguing the network spends too much time highlighting Democrats and not his accomplishments.

Republicans were handed major losses in the House and Senate on Tuesday, setting up a clash with the president during his last two years in office.

images.caption: Sean Hannity listens as President Trump speaks during the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) first-ever midterm convention on Sept. 9, 2026, in Dallas.

articles.title: Deb Haaland wins New Mexico governor’s race
articles.summary: Democrat Deb Haaland is projected to defeat her Republican opponent Gregg Hull in New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Haaland, who served as Interior secretary under former President Biden, will become the first Native American woman to serve as governor of a U.S. state. She previously made history as one of…
articles.body:
Democrat Deb Haaland is projected to defeat her Republican opponent Gregg Hull in New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Haaland, who served as Interior secretary under former President Biden, will become the first Native American woman to serve as governor of a U.S. state. She previously made history as one of the first two Native Americans elected to Congress in 2018.

DDHQ projected that Haaland defeated Hull by almost 12 percentage points with 37 percent of votes counted as of 10:33 p.m. EST.

She will succeed term-limited Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham (D), keeping the governor’s mansion in Democratic hands.

Haaland, a member of the Laguna Pueblo, previously represented New Mexico’s 1st Congressional District before joining the Biden administration in 2021. As Interior chief, she oversaw federal public lands and conservation efforts, as well as an investigation into abuses at Native American boarding schools.

Hull served three terms as mayor of Rio Rancho, New Mexico’s third-largest city. He campaigned on improving public safety, expanding economic opportunities and reforming education.

Affordability was a central issue in the race, with Haaland proposing to raise the minimum wage, expand tax credits for working families and increase housing construction. She also campaigned on expanding access to healthcare, protecting Medicaid and strengthening New Mexico’s universal childcare program.

The two candidates differed sharply over President Trump’s policies, with Haaland criticizing the administration’s handling of the economy and Hull arguing that Democratic leadership had failed to address the Land of Enchantment’s challenges.

New Mexico voters last elected a GOP governor in 2014, when former Gov. Susana Martinez won reelection.

Ahead of Election Day, DDHQ gave Haaland an 87 percent chance of winning.

articles.body:
Democrat Don Leonard is projected to win Ohio’s 15th District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Leonard defeated incumbent Rep. Mike Carey (R-Ohio), delivering Democrats a pickup in a district Republicans have held for more than a decade.

DDHQ projected that Leonard beat Carey by almost 8 percentage points with 91 percent of ballots cast at 10:37 p.m. EST.

The result marks a political breakthrough for Leonard, an Ohio State University professor who entered the race hoping to turn voter frustration over the cost of living into support for his first congressional bid.

It also brings an end to Carey’s five years in Washington.

The Republican, a former coal lobbyist, first won the seat in a 2021 special election with President Trump’s backing. He went on to win reelection twice, most recently defeating his Democratic challenger by roughly 13 percentage points in 2024.

But Democrats saw an opportunity in the Columbus-area district as they worked to expand the House battlefield beyond traditional swing seats.

Leonard made affordability and access to healthcare central to his campaign, frequently pointing to his upbringing in a financially struggling family.

The Democrat also brought an unconventional resume to the race. Before becoming a professor of city and regional planning at Ohio State University, Leonard served in the Peace Corps in South America and earned a doctorate in government from Cornell University.

Carey campaigned on his experience in Congress, including his work on the House Ways and Means Committee, and his support for Trump’s policies.

Leonard won the Democratic nomination in May, defeating former state Rep. Adam Miller.

DHHQ rated the district “likely Republican” heading into Election Day.

Rep. Scott Perry (R-Pa.), an ally to President Trump, is projected to lose to Democratic opponent Janelle Stelson, according to The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Perry has represented Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District since 2018. Now, Stelson has flipped one of the most highly contested seats in the Keystone State blue.

She lost to Perry in the 2024 election for the district’s seat, but only by a little more than 1 point — about 5,000 votes.

With nearly 80 percent of the ballots counted around 10:45 p.m. EST Tuesday, Stelson was up on Perry by 13 points, according to DDHQ .

The Democratic candidate worked for WGAL-TV in Lancaster, Pa., as a reporter before leaving to run for Congress in 2023. Originally registered as a Republican , she switched her affiliation for her run for Congress.

Stelson had pledged in her campaign to work with Republicans and Democrats on issues such as rising housing and healthcare costs, supporting small business owners and assisting Pennsylvania’s agriculture.

She received endorsements from some of the state’s top Democrats including Gov. Josh Shapiro and Lt. Gov. Austin Davis.

articles.title: Figures defends redrawn Alabama House seat in major victory for Democrats
articles.summary: Alabama Rep. Shomari Figures (D) is projected to win a second term on Capitol Hill in a major blow to the GOP, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Figures defeated GOP state Rep. Rhett Marques for the red-leaning 2nd District seat in the Montgomery, Ala., area. Marques was the favorite to win after the Supreme…
articles.body:
Alabama Rep. Shomari Figures (D) is projected to win a second term on Capitol Hill in a major blow to the GOP, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Figures defeated GOP state Rep. Rhett Marques for the red-leaning 2nd District seat in the Montgomery, Ala., area. Marques was the favorite to win after the Supreme Court reinstated a 2023 map this spring, redrawing the majority-Black district and giving Republicans an upper hand. DDHQ forecasted the seat was “likely” to flip.

Democrats across the country blasted the May decision, which came just days after the high court narrowed the landmark Voting Rights Act.

“I don’t view it as me paying the price, I view it as voters who I represent, and Black voters particularly, I think, paying the price because they are having a legitimate opportunity to have representation in Congress,” Figures told The Hill in June.

Marques notched endorsements from President Trump and House Republican leadership, including Speaker Mike Johnson (La.).

His loss delivers a blow to Trump and the GOP after the party sought to cushion its margins in the lower chamber by redrawing House districts to favor it. A number of states, including Texas, Florida and Tennessee, were redistricted to boost the party ahead of the 2026 midterms.

Alabama’s district lines were changed due to a court decision in favor of maps established prior to the national redistricting war sparked by Trump. Still, Figures’s victory underscores Democratic enthusiasm amid Republicans’ souring approval.

The Democrat was first elected in 2024, and he previously worked in the Obama and Biden administrations. He currently serves on the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Agriculture Committee.

articles.title: Adam Hamilton flips Senate seat blue in Kansas
articles.summary: Adam Hamilton, a Democrat and pastor, is projected to win the Senate race in Kansas, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), all but ensuring a Senate majority for his party. Hamilton will unseat incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R) and flip a seat that was once expected to be safe for the GOP. He will be the…
articles.body:
Adam Hamilton, a Democrat and pastor , is projected to win the Senate race in Kansas, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), all but ensuring a Senate majority for his party.

Hamilton will unseat incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R) and flip a seat that was once expected to be safe for the GOP. He will be the first Democratic senator from the Sunflower State since 1939.

DDHQ projected that Hamilton beat Marshall by almost 9 percentage points with 87 percent of votes cast as of 10:48 p.m. EST.

It’s another massive victory for Democratic Senate candidates in a cycle in which the party has already been projected as winning seats in Texas and South Carolina.

Kansas had seemed like a long shot, but the party had one of its strongest candidates in Hamilton, 62, a Methodist pastor who gathered a surge of fundraising and energy around him after winning the August primary .

Hamilton leaned into his experience as founding pastor of the largest Methodist church in the country. He picked up endorsements from prominent Republicans in the state, including two former governors.

Hamilton also benefitted from missteps by Marshall, who earlier this fall defended the economy as strong.

Marshall also struggled after a New York Times story said he had sued a number of patients over minor medical debts, some of who ended up being arrested.

The incumbent filmed a video defending himself that became public at the beginning of this week. It was a video his own advisers reportedly suggested he not release.

Marshall also suffered from a rough political environment for Republicans as popular opinion continued to sour on President Trump and the war in Iran . And while Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in a century, several recent governors have been Democrats.

Marshall and national Republicans looked to target Hamilton’s faith as “woke,” running ads that splice quotes from Hamilton’s sermons to suggest he believes white privilege and eating meat are sinful.

But Hamilton was already well known in Kansas from his work as a pastor and author, and he channeled his mild manner and strong speaking skills to appeal to disillusioned Republicans and independents along with Democrats. He also distanced himself from the Democratic establishment, saying he would not support Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as majority leader if elected and critiquing the Biden administration for its handling of the southern border.

DDHQ rated the seat as a “toss-up” going into Election Day.

articles.title: Democrat Benson wins race to succeed Whitmer in Michigan
articles.summary: Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D) is projected to defeat Republican Rep. John James in the state’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). articles.body:
Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D) is projected to defeat Republican Rep. John James in the state’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Benson was leading by 11 percentage points — 55 percent to 44 percent — with 31 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 10:45 p.m. EST.

Benson, who was first elected secretary of state in 2018, will succeed outgoing Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D), who is term limited. Benson’s victory breaks Michigan’s decades-long pattern of switching parties in the governor’s office after eight years.

Benson gained national attention in 2020 for defending Michigan’s presidential election results against President Trump’s efforts to overturn his loss.

As the state’s chief election official, she also faced threats and harassment, including armed protesters who gathered outside her home to demand the results be overturned. Her actions earned her the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award in 2022 and the Presidential Citizens Medal in 2023.

A former law school dean and civil rights activist, Benson campaigned on lowering costs and protecting abortion rights and voting access. She sought to tie James to Trump’s tariffs and attacked his congressional record on healthcare.

James, a West Point graduate and Army veteran, campaigned on economic issues, blaming Democratic leadership in the state for higher costs and slow growth. He secured Trump’s endorsement in the GOP primary, which helped him defeat businessman Perry Johnson, who spent nearly $33 million of his own money on the campaign, according to Cook Political Report.

The result marks James’s third unsuccessful statewide bid in recent years. He lost Senate races to former Sen. Debbie Stabenow (D-Mich.) in 2018 and Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) in 2020. He subsequently ran for a competitive House seat and served two terms before running for governor.

Benson entered the final days of the campaign as the favorite, with DDHQ rating the race “likely Democrat” and giving Benson a 78 percent chance of winning as of Friday. The election handicapper’s polling average also showed Benson leading James, 49.8 percent to 42 percent.

The contest shifted in Benson’s favor once former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan, an independent candidate, dropped out in May. His withdrawal from the race led Cook Political Report to move the race from toss-up to “lean Democrat.”

On the campaign trail, Benson faced scrutiny over her husband’s work for a data center developer. She called for a statewide moratorium on the developments, while James pushed for local governments to have the power to block them.

articles.title: Kristi Noem blames GOP election results on Trump’s first year successes
articles.summary: Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said Tuesday the second Trump administration was “too successful” in its first year, a comment which came as unfavorable GOP election outcomes rolled in. The post from Noem, who was removed from her role after overseeing Trump’s aggressive immigration agenda, directly responded to Fox Business host Larry Kudlow’s comment…
articles.body:
Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said Tuesday the second Trump administration was “too successful” in its first year, a comment which came as unfavorable GOP election outcomes rolled in.

The post from Noem, who was removed from her role after overseeing Trump’s aggressive immigration agenda, directly responded to Fox Business host Larry Kudlow’s comment similarly attributing Republican midterm losses to the administration’s success.

“Larry Kudlow is correct. We were too successful the first year of the Trump administration,” Noem wrote in a post to social platform X.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, projected just after 9 p.m. that Democrats would take control of the House. The party is also encroaching on the Senate, as DDHQ called tight races in South Carolina, Texas and North Carolina for Democratic candidates.

As DHS secretary, Noem oversaw U.S. Customs and Border Protection, as well as Immigration and Customs Enforcement. She held the post during the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis at the start of this year, which led to the deaths of two American citizens.

Backlash surrounding Trump’s deportation push may have contributed to GOP losses in states with large Latino populations — a group which has historically ranked immigration as a key issue at the polls. For example, Texas — which is around 41 percent Hispanic-Latino — elected a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1988.
